publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: how general anesthetics abolish consciousness, and whether the states they produce are unconsciousness or only unresponsiveness and amnesia
span.quote: Although anesthesia undoubtedly induces unresponsiveness and amnesia, the extent to which it causes unconsciousness is harder to establish.

span.label: when we are anesthetized, does consciousness always vanish — and what neural change is the one that actually removes it
span.quote: When we are anesthetized, we expect consciousness to vanish. But does it always?

span.label: argues that anesthetics remove consciousness when they block the integration of information — either by disconnecting the posterior corticothalamic complex or by collapsing its repertoire of states — and that the field's behavioural test cannot tell unconsciousness from unresponsiveness
span.quote: Thus, anesthetics seem to cause unconsciousness when they block the brain’s ability to integrate information.

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Thus, anesthetics seem to cause unconsciousness when they block the brain’s ability to integrate information.

span.label: anesthetic-induced unconsciousness
span.quote: Consciousness vanishes when anesthetics produce functional disconnection in this posterior complex, interrupting cortical communication and causing a loss of integration; or when they lead to bistable, stereotypic responses, causing a loss of information capacity.

span.label: review
span.quote: The evidence from anesthesia and sleep states ( Fig. 2 – 3 ) converges to suggest that loss of consciousness is associated with a breakdown of cortical connectivity and thus of integration, or with a collapse of the repertoire of cortical activity patterns and thus of information ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Anesthetics abolish consciousness by blocking the corticothalamic system's capacity to integrate information, not simply by silencing neurons
span.quote: Thus, anesthetics seem to cause unconsciousness when they block the brain’s ability to integrate information.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because the corticothalamic system is a small-world network, cutting only a few long-range connections fragments it into functionally disconnected components
span.quote: By the same token, anesthetics need only disrupt a few long-range connections to produce a set of disconnected components.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Deep anesthesia collapses the response repertoire into a stereotypic two-state burst-suppression regime, so activity carries almost no information even while remaining globally integrated
span.quote: However, the repertoire of responses has shrunk to a stereotypic burst-suppression pattern, with a corresponding loss of information, essentially creating a system having only two possible states (on or off).

span.label: two independent routes to unconsciousness are proposed, so that a brain can fail either by disconnecting or by running out of things to say
span.quote: According to this framework, anesthetics would produce unconsciousness either by preventing integration (blocking the interactions among specialized brain regions) or by reducing information (shrinking the number of activity patterns available to cortical networks).

span.label: burst-suppression is the crucial counterexample to activity-based accounts: the system is active, hyperexcitable and globally integrated, and still unconscious, because its repertoire has fallen to two states
span.quote: Thus, during deep anesthetic unconsciousness the corticothalamic system can still be active in fact hyperexcitable and can produce global, integrated responses. However, the repertoire of responses has shrunk to a stereotypic burst-suppression pattern, with a corresponding loss of information, essentially creating a system having only two possible states (on or off).

span.label: a causal role for the thalamus is demoted to a readout by a timing argument: cortical EEG changes at the instant of loss of consciousness, thalamic EEG only ten minutes later
span.quote: the cortical EEG changed dramatically the instant the patients lost consciousness ( 38 ). However, there was little change in thalamic EEG activity until 10 minutes later.

span.label: unresponsiveness is separated from unconsciousness by existence proofs rather than by measurement: dreaming and pharmacological paralysis are states with experience and without response
span.quote: When we dream, we have vivid conscious experiences, but are unresponsive because inhibition by the brainstem induces muscle paralysis ( 13 ).

span.label: amnesia is separated from unconsciousness the same way: the isolated forearm technique buys a channel of report that survives paralysis, and patients use it and then deny having been awake
span.quote: Studies with the isolated forearm technique, in which a tourniquet is applied to the arm before paralysis is induced (to allow the hand to move while the rest of the body is paralyzed), show that patients under general anesthesia can sometimes carry on a conversation using hand signals, but post-operatively deny ever being awake ( 21 ).

span.label: TMS is used as a perturbation probe: push the cortex and measure how far and how specifically the response travels, which turns integration into something measurable rather than inferred from correlation
span.quote: During wakefulness, transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) applied to premotor cortex and other cortical areas induces a sustained response (300 ms) involving the sequential activation of specific brain areas, the identity of which depends upon the precise site of stimulation ( 63 , 64 ).

span.label: convergence across two unrelated ways of losing consciousness — anesthesia and slow-wave sleep — is what carries the argument, since neither alone would isolate the common factor
span.quote: The evidence from anesthesia and sleep states ( Fig. 2 – 3 ) converges to suggest that loss of consciousness is associated with a breakdown of cortical connectivity and thus of integration, or with a collapse of the repertoire of cortical activity patterns and thus of information ( Fig. 2 ).

span.label: network topology explains the disproportion between a small pharmacological insult and a total loss of consciousness: in a small-world graph a few long-range edges hold the whole thing together
span.quote: By the same token, anesthetics need only disrupt a few long-range connections to produce a set of disconnected components.

span.label: lesion data and anesthesia data are used as mutual corroboration, on the argument that a drug and a knife reaching the same region should produce the same deficit
span.quote: In this case, lesion and anesthesia data are mutually supportive: patients with bilateral lesions at the temporo-parieto-occipital junction show no sign of perceptual experience, despite a flurry of undirected motor activity, a condition called hyperkinetic mutism ( 18 ).

span.label: a theory is used to license a negative rule of inference, forbidding both directions of the usual behavioural reading
span.quote: The theory suggests that one should not interpret individual motor responses, or localized activations, as signs of consciousness, and conversely should not interpret the absence of motor responses as a sure sign of unconsciousness.

span.label: the die metaphor is doing real theoretical work, not decoration: it makes 'integration' and 'information' visibly separable — a die that disintegrates versus a die that is flattened
span.quote: The corticothalamic system is represented metaphorically as a large die having many faces, each corresponding to a different brain firing pattern.

span.label: The integrated-information measure the paper's framework rests on cannot at present be computed for real brains, only for small simulated systems.
span.quote: In practice, Φ can only be measured rigorously for small, simulated systems.

span.label: The paper cannot settle which component of the posterior complex matters most, nor the role of anterior cortex.
span.quote: Whether the medial or lateral component is more important, and whether anterior cortical regions are critical primarily for executive functions and perhaps self-reflection, remain questions for future work.

span.label: the measure the theory rests on cannot be computed for a brain
span.quote: In practice, Φ can only be measured rigorously for small, simulated systems.

span.label: the paper opens by conceding that the thing it is explaining the loss of is itself unexplained
span.quote: How consciousness arises in the brain remains unknown.

span.label: which part of the posterior complex matters is left open
span.quote: Whether the medial or lateral component is more important, and whether anterior cortical regions are critical primarily for executive functions and perhaps self-reflection, remain questions for future work.

span.label: the existing monitors fail exactly where they are needed, at the transition
span.quote: but they remain limited at directly indicating the presence or absence of consciousness, especially around the transition point

span.label: a disjunction the paper cannot resolve: the signal may be wrong, or the interpretation may be
span.quote: Either the EEG is not sensitive enough to the neural processes underlying consciousness, or we still do not yet fully understand what to look for.

span.label: the candidate region is deactivated in REM sleep, when experience is vivid — the paper states the counterexample to its own anatomy without resolving it
span.quote: Nevertheless, mesial cortical areas are deactivated in REM sleep ( 48 ), when subjects experience vivid dreams.

span.label: selective deactivation of the candidate posterior region produces altered experience, not absent experience
span.quote: yet when these areas start to turn off, subjects report dreamlike feelings with depersonalization and out of body experiences, rather than unconsciousness

span.label: the classical measurement of information as reduction of uncertainty in bits, applied to brain states and conscious experience
span.quote: Classically, information is the reduction of uncertainty among alternatives: when a coin falls on one of its two sides, it provides 1 bit of information, whereas a die falling on one of six faces provides ~2.6 bits.

span.label: the bit and the reduction of uncertainty among alternatives, imported wholesale as the measure of how much experience a brain state constitutes
span.quote: Classically, information is the reduction of uncertainty among alternatives: when a coin falls on one of its two sides, it provides 1 bit of information, whereas a die falling on one of six faces provides ~2.6 bits.

span.label: small-world topology, used to explain why a small pharmacological insult to a few long-range connections can fragment the whole system
span.quote: Small-world networks have mostly local connectivity with comparatively few long-range connections. Augmented with hubs, such networks maximize interactions while minimizing wiring.

span.label: transfer entropy, borrowed as a directional measure so that feedforward and feedback interactions can be scored separately
span.quote: transfer entropy, a measure of directional interactions among brain areas, is balanced in the feedforward (green) and feedback (red) directions

span.label: the die as a model of a state repertoire, extended so that losing integration shatters it into many dice and losing information flattens it to two faces
span.quote: If integration is lost (as in anesthesia or sleep), the die disintegrates into many two-faced dice, each generating 1 bit of information.

span.label: information
span.quote: the repertoire of responses has shrunk to a stereotypic burst-suppression pattern, with a corresponding loss of information, essentially creating a system having only two possible states (on or off)

span.label: burst-suppression
span.quote: the repertoire of responses has shrunk to a stereotypic burst-suppression pattern, with a corresponding loss of information, essentially creating a system having only two possible states (on or off)

span.label: unconsciousness — behavioural sense: failing to move on command, the 160-year-old clinical criterion
span.quote: At slightly higher doses, a patient fails to move in response to a command and is considered unconscious.

span.label: unconsciousness — experiential sense: absence of experience, which the behavioural criterion does not track
span.quote: Thus, clinical unresponsiveness is not necessarily synonymous with unconsciousness.

span.label: information — classical sense: reduction of uncertainty among alternatives, measured in bits
span.quote: Classically, information is the reduction of uncertainty among alternatives: when a coin falls on one of its two sides, it provides 1 bit of information, whereas a die falling on one of six faces provides ~2.6 bits.

span.label: information — the paper's working sense: the number of discriminable activity patterns a neural system can produce
span.quote: Consider now how anesthetics affect information, defined loosely as the number of discriminable activity patterns.

span.label: integration — the ability of different cortical regions to interact effectively, explicitly flagged as a loose definition
span.quote: Consider first large-scale integration, loosely defined as the ability of different cortical regions to interact effectively ( 52 )

span.label: consciousness — graded, increasing with the repertoire of discriminable states, not all-or-none
span.quote: consciousness is not an all-or-none property, but it is graded: specifically, it increases in proportion to a system’s repertoire of discriminable states.

span.label: thalamus — as a switch that gates consciousness, versus as a readout of cortical state; the paper names both and argues for the second
span.quote: Thus, the effects of anesthetics on the thalamus effect may represent a readout of global cortical activity rather than a consciousness switch, and thalamic activity may not be a sufficient basis for consciousness.

span.label: down-state — local, induced under one TMS site, versus global, induced across the connectional core; the same term at two scales in one paragraph
span.quote: This stereotypic response, presumably due to the simultaneous activation of the cortical connectional core and to the induction of a global down state, reflects a limited repertoire of activity patterns and thus a loss of information.

span.label: anesthetics — two classes by clinical role: intravenous agents to induce, volatile agents to maintain
span.quote: General anesthetics fall into two main classes: intravenous agents used to induce anesthesia, generally administered together with sedatives or narcotics; and volatile agents, generally used for anesthesia maintenance ( Table 1 )

span.label: loss of consciousness — as an abrupt threshold crossing, versus as a shrinking or dimming; the paper says the evidence shows both
span.quote: The shrinking or dimming of the field of consciousness during sedation is consistent with this idea. On the other hand, the abrupt loss of consciousness at a critical concentration of anesthetics suggests that the integrated repertoire of neural states underlying consciousness may collapse non-linearly.

span.label: critiques → the behavioural definition of unconsciousness that anesthesia has used since its introduction
span.quote: This behavioral definition of unconsciousness, which was introduced with anesthesia over 160 years ago, while convenient, has drawbacks.

span.label: critiques → the thalamic switch hypothesis (ref 2), that the thalamus gates consciousness
span.quote: Thus, the effects of anesthetics on the thalamus effect may represent a readout of global cortical activity rather than a consciousness switch, and thalamic activity may not be a sufficient basis for consciousness.

span.label: supports → the integrated information theory of consciousness (ref 52)
span.quote: A recent theory suggests a principled reason: information and integration may be the very essence of consciousness ( 52 ).

span.label: contradicts → the clinical inference from absent motor response to absent consciousness
span.quote: The theory suggests that one should not interpret individual motor responses, or localized activations, as signs of consciousness, and conversely should not interpret the absence of motor responses as a sure sign of unconsciousness.

span.label: extends → existing depth-of-anesthesia monitoring, by proposing monitors that measure integration and information separately
span.quote: This approach could allow the development of consciousness monitors that evaluate both loss of integration, as revealed by reduced functional or effective connectivity, and loss of information, as evidenced by stereotypic responses.

span.label: supports → rival frameworks — global workspace and coalitions of neurons — which the paper declines to argue against
span.quote: Other frameworks for consciousness, emphasizing access to a global workspace ( 65 , 66 ), or the formation of large coalitions of neurons ( 43 ), are also consistent with many of the findings described here, especially those concerning the role of cortical integration.

span.label: unresponsiveness —distinct-from→ unconsciousness
span.quote: Thus, clinical unresponsiveness is not necessarily synonymous with unconsciousness.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · amnesia —distinct-from→ unconsciousness
span.note: RETRACTED: RE-GROUNDED. The old span named only unconsciousness. This sentence names both and distinguishes them ON THE EVIDENCE AVAILABLE FOR EACH - anaesthesia 'undoubtedly induces ... amnesia' while the extent to which it causes unconsciousness 'is harder to establish'.
span.quote: Thus, retrospective oblivion is no proof of unconsciousness.

span.label: integrated information —same-as→ consciousness
span.quote: A recent theory suggests a principled reason: information and integration may be the very essence of consciousness ( 52 ).

span.label: integrated information —operationalised-as→ phi
span.quote: A measure of integrated information, called phi (Φ), can be used to quantify the information generated when a system enters one particular state of its repertoire, above and beyond the information generated independently by its parts ( 52 ).

span.label: integration —operationalised-as→ transfer entropy
span.quote: During waking, transfer entropy, a measure of directional interactions among brain areas, is balanced in the feedforward (green) and feedback (red) directions.

span.label: thalamus —distinct-from→ consciousness switch
span.quote: Thus, the effects of anesthetics on the thalamus effect may represent a readout of global cortical activity rather than a consciousness switch, and thalamic activity may not be a sufficient basis for consciousness.

span.label: burst-suppression —causes→ information
span.quote: the repertoire of responses has shrunk to a stereotypic burst-suppression pattern, with a corresponding loss of information, essentially creating a system having only two possible states (on or off)

span.label: up-state —distinct-from→ down-state
span.quote: At intermediate anesthetic concentrations, neurons begin oscillating, roughly once a second, between a depolarized up-state and a hyperpolarized down-state ( 11 ).

span.label: corticothalamic system —is-a→ small-world
span.quote: The corticothalamic system may be especially vulnerable to anesthetics due to its small-world organization.

span.label: cerebellum —contrasted-with→ corticothalamic system
span.quote: By contrast, parts of the brain made up of small, quasi-independent modules, such as the cerebellum, and parallel loops through the basal ganglia, are not sufficiently integrated, which is perhaps why they can be lesioned without loss of consciousness ( 18 , 52 ).

span.label: depth of anesthesia —operationalised-as→ bispectral index
span.quote: bispectral index monitors record the EEG signal over the forehead and reduce the complex signal into a single number that tracks a patient’s depth of anesthesia over time ( 12 )

span.label: global workspace —distinct-from→ integrated information
span.quote: Other frameworks for consciousness, emphasizing access to a global workspace ( 65 , 66 ), or the formation of large coalitions of neurons ( 43 ), are also consistent with many of the findings described here, especially those concerning the role of cortical integration.

span.label: propofol —contrasted-with→ thiopental
span.quote: For instance, at equivalent hypnotic doses, both propofol and thiopental deactivate posterior brain areas, but only propofol deactivates frontal cortex ( 44 ).

span.label: slow wave sleep —contrasted-with→ anesthesia
span.quote: Although anesthesia is not the same as natural sleep, brain arousal systems are similarly deactivated ( 6 , 62 ).

span.label: mesial cortical areas —part-of→ default network
span.quote: These mesial cortical areas are strategically located at the main hub of the brain’s connectional core ( 49 ). They are also part of a default network that is especially active at rest and may be involved in global monitoring of the internal environment and several functions related to the self ( 50 ).

span.label: amnesia —distinct-from→ unconsciousness
span.note: RE-GROUNDS Alkire2008-consciousness-and-anesthesia[1]: the old span named ONE endpoint.
span.quote: Although anesthesia undoubtedly induces unresponsiveness and amnesia, the extent to which it causes unconsciousness is harder to establish.

span.label: Most anesthetics produce unconsciousness by acting, directly or indirectly, on a posterior lateral corticothalamic complex around the inferior parietal lobe rather than on the whole brain uniformly.
span.quote: Despite different mechanisms and sites of action, most anesthetic agents appear to cause unconsciousness by targeting, directly or indirectly, a posterior lateral corticothalamic complex centered around the inferior parietal lobe, and perhaps a medial cortical core.

span.label: The thalamic deactivation seen under anesthesia is better interpreted as a readout of cortical state than as the switch that turns consciousness off.
span.quote: Thus, the effects of anesthetics on the thalamus effect may represent a readout of global cortical activity rather than a consciousness switch, and thalamic activity may not be a sufficient basis for consciousness.

span.label: Behavioural unresponsiveness under anesthesia does not reliably indicate that the patient is unconscious.
span.quote: Thus, clinical unresponsiveness is not necessarily synonymous with unconsciousness.

span.label: Post-operative amnesia is likewise not evidence that the patient was unconscious during surgery.
span.quote: Thus, retrospective oblivion is no proof of unconsciousness.

span.label: Evidence from both anesthesia and sleep converges on two routes to unconsciousness: loss of cortical integration or collapse of the repertoire of cortical activity patterns.
span.quote: loss of consciousness is associated with a breakdown of cortical connectivity and thus of integration, or with a collapse of the repertoire of cortical activity patterns and thus of information

span.label: On the integrated-information account, consciousness is graded rather than all-or-none, scaling with the size of a system's repertoire of discriminable states.
span.quote: Finally, from this theoretical perspective, consciousness is not an all-or-none property, but it is graded: specifically, it increases in proportion to a system’s repertoire of discriminable states.

span.label: intraoperative awareness occurs about once in every 1000–2000 operations
span.quote: once in every 1000–2000 operations a patient may temporarily regain consciousness or even remain conscious during surgery ( 1 )

span.label: sevoflurane sedation cuts relative thalamic metabolism by 23% in subjects who are still awake and responsive, so thalamic reduction is not sufficient for unconsciousness
span.quote: sevoflurane sedation causes a 23% reduction of relative thalamic metabolism when subjects are still awake and responsive ( 30 )

span.label: cortical EEG changed at the instant of loss of consciousness while thalamic EEG did not change for another ten minutes
span.quote: the cortical EEG changed dramatically the instant the patients lost consciousness ( 38 ). However, there was little change in thalamic EEG activity until 10 minutes later.

span.label: in REM sleep the two dissociate the other way: cortical EEG activated as if awake, thalamic EEG showing slow waves as if asleep
span.quote: in epileptic patients, during REM sleep (usually associated with dreaming) the cortical EEG was activated as if awake, but the thalamic EEG showed slow wave activity as if asleep ( 39 )

span.label: after thalamic ablation the cortex still produces an activated EEG
span.quote: after thalamic ablation, the cortex still produces an activated EEG ( 37 )

span.label: the thalamic effects of anesthetics disappear if the cortex is removed, which makes them look consequent on cortical deactivation
span.quote: the metabolic and electrophysiological effects of anesthetics on the thalamus in animals are abolished by removal of the cortex ( 33 , 34 , 36 )

span.label: ketamine raises global metabolism, especially thalamic, going the opposite way from every other agent
span.quote: Ketamine increases global metabolism, especially in the thalamus ( 16 ).

span.label: propofol and thiopental both deactivate posterior areas at equivalent hypnotic doses but only propofol deactivates frontal cortex, so frontal deactivation is not required
span.quote: For instance, at equivalent hypnotic doses, both propofol and thiopental deactivate posterior brain areas, but only propofol deactivates frontal cortex ( 44 ).

span.label: large frontal lesions do not by themselves produce unconsciousness
span.quote: Furthermore, large lesions of the frontal cortex do not by themselves produce unconsciousness ( 45 ).

span.label: a clinically unresponsive woman with large frontal lesions produced cortical activation patterns indistinguishable from healthy subjects when asked to imagine playing tennis
span.quote: a woman with large frontal lesions who was clinically unresponsive was asked to imagine playing tennis or to navigate her room and she showed cortical activation patterns indistinguishable from those of healthy subjects ( 19 )

span.label: as consciousness fades, EEG coherence in the gamma range drops between the two frontal cortices and between frontal and occipital regions
span.quote: When consciousness fades during anesthesia there is a drop in EEG coherence in the γ frequency range (20 to 80 Hz) between right and left frontal cortices and between frontal and occipital regions ( 4 ).

span.label: the coherence loss is far stronger for long-range than for local connections
span.quote: The effect is gradual and much stronger for long-range than for local coherence ( 53 ).

span.label: in rats losing responsiveness, information transfer falls in the feedback direction first
span.quote: When rats become unresponsive under anesthesia, information transfer first decreases in the feedback direction ( Fig. 3 ) ( 56 ).

span.label: anesthesia suppresses the late component of visual responses but not the early feedforward one, and abolishes contextual and attentional modulation
span.quote: Also, anesthesia suppresses the late component (>100 ms) of visual responses, possibly by inhibiting feedback connections ( 57 ), but not the early feedforward components. Moreover, anesthesia abolishes contextual and attentional modulation of firing, presumably mediated by feedback connections ( 58 ).

span.label: TMS during waking evokes a 300 ms sequential response whose identity depends on the stimulation site; in early non-REM sleep the same pulse produces a short local response under 150 ms
span.quote: During early non-REM sleep, presumably due to the induction of a local down-state, TMS pulses produce instead a short (<150 ms) local response ( 64 ), suggesting a loss of integration.

span.label: TMS to mesial parietal cortex, over the main connectional hub, triggers a stereotypic high-amplitude slow wave closely resembling a spontaneous one
span.quote: Intriguingly, TMS pulses to mesial parietal regions, overlying the main hub in the cortical connectional core ( 49 ), trigger a stereotypic, high-amplitude slow wave closely resembling spontaneous slow waves ( 63 ).

span.label: nitrous oxide at intermediate doses selectively deactivates posterior mesial cortex, yet subjects report dreamlike experience rather than none
span.quote: It is intriguing that at intermediate doses, certain anesthetics, such as nitrous oxide, produce a fairly selective deactivation of posterior mesial cortex ( 51 ), yet when these areas start to turn off, subjects report dreamlike feelings with depersonalization and out of body experiences, rather than unconsciousness.

span.label: generalized convulsive seizures lose consciousness with high, hypersynchronous activity — integration intact, repertoire stereotypic
span.quote: Generalized convulsive seizures provide another example in which consciousness can be lost even though neural activity remains high and highly synchronized: a large portion of the corticothalamic complex is engaged in strong, hypersynchronous activity, but this activity is stereotypic ( 60 , 61 ).

span.label: GABA agonists in the intralaminar nuclei put rats to sleep, and nicotine there wakes them from sevoflurane — the switch-like evidence the paper then qualifies
span.quote: For example, GABA agonists (mimicking anesthetic action) injected into the intralaminar nuclei cause rats to rapidly fall asleep, with a corresponding slowing of the EEG ( 26 ). Conversely, rats under anesthetic concentrations of sevoflurane can be awakened by a minute injection of nicotine into the intralaminar thalamus ( 27 ).

span.label: computer simulations show a rapid state transition at a critical anesthetic dose, matching the abruptness of clinical loss of consciousness
span.quote: Indeed, computer simulations demonstrate a rapid state transition at a critical anesthetic dose ( 59 ), consistent with a breakdown in network integration.

span.label: patients can be aware and responsive during surgery while the bispectral index says otherwise
span.quote: The isolated forearm technique has shown that individual patients can be aware and responsive during surgery even though their bispectral index value suggests they are not ( 25 ).

span.label: integrated information (phi, Φ)
span.quote: A measure of integrated information, called phi (Φ), can be used to quantify the information generated when a system enters one particular state of its repertoire, above and beyond the information generated independently by its parts

span.label: information (as the number of discriminable activity patterns)

span.quote: the electroencephalogram (EEG) (electrical recording from the scalp)

span.label: down-state
span.quote: The down-state shows complete cessation of synaptic activity for a tenth of a second or more, after which neurons revert to another up-state.

span.label: flat EEG
span.quote: a flat EEG [indicating the cessation of the brain’s electrical activity, one of the criteria for brain death ( 22 )]

span.label: information
span.quote: Classically, information is the reduction of uncertainty among alternatives

span.label: once in every 1000–2000 operations — rate at which a surgical patient regains or retains consciousness under general anesthesia (intraoperative awareness)
span.quote: once in every 1000–2000 operations a patient may temporarily regain consciousness or even remain conscious during surgery

span.label: 23% — reduction of relative thalamic metabolism under sevoflurane sedation in subjects who are still awake and responsive, showing thalamic suppression is not sufficient for unconsciousness
span.quote: sevoflurane sedation causes a 23% reduction of relative thalamic metabolism when subjects are still awake and responsive

span.label: once in every 1000–2000 operations — rate of intraoperative awareness

span.label: over 160 years — age of the behavioural definition of unconsciousness
span.quote: This behavioral definition of unconsciousness, which was introduced with anesthesia over 160 years ago, while convenient, has drawbacks.

span.label: 23% — reduction of relative thalamic metabolism under sevoflurane sedation in awake responsive subjects
span.quote: a 23% reduction of relative thalamic metabolism when subjects are still awake and responsive

span.label: 10 minutes — lag between the cortical EEG change at loss of consciousness and any thalamic change
span.quote: there was little change in thalamic EEG activity until 10 minutes later

span.label: 20 to 80 Hz — gamma range in which coherence drops as consciousness fades
span.quote: a drop in EEG coherence in the γ frequency range (20 to 80 Hz)

span.label: 20 to 60 Hz — gamma range of the flash-evoked response in rat occipital cortex
span.quote: each flash evokes a sustained gamma frequency (20 to 60 Hz) response in visual occipital cortex

span.label: 300 ms — duration of the sequential TMS-evoked response during wakefulness

span.label: >100 ms — the late visual response component that anesthesia suppresses
span.quote: anesthesia suppresses the late component (>100 ms) of visual responses

span.label: 1 Hz or less — frequency of the slow oscillation between up- and down-states in slow wave sleep

span.label: 1.1% isoflurane — anesthetic concentration in the rat flash-response experiment
span.quote: from a representative rat when awake and under 1.1% isoflurane anesthesia

span.label: 0.2 Hz — rate of the flashing light stimulus
span.quote: Responses to a flashing light delivered at 0.2 Hz (arrow)

span.quote: whereas a die falling on one of six faces provides ~2.6 bits
